titleStmt.title: A Short History of Birds and Beasts, for the Amusement and Instruction of Children.
titleStmt.author: Anonymous
titleStmt.editor: Audrey Goddard, Phoebe Norton, and Marin Tisdale

publicationStmt.p: We are interested in this particular text because of how it combines visual and textual elements in a format intended for younger audiences. In other words, we are interested in the intersection between the physicality of the text in relation to its audience, and how this relationship can evolve over time. By preserving our text, we hope to offer insight into the historical evolution of children’s literature in order to better understand the factors contributing to such change.

sourceDesc.p: A Short History of Birds and Beasts is a 19th century children's chapbook created for children to both entertain and instill moral teachings. It is written in both prose and verse with entries for thirteen different animals accompanied by corresponding illustrations. This chapbook is accessible through the UW Libraries: physically in their special collections and digitally through Project Gutenberg. A Short History of Birds and Beasts Anonymous Wellington, Salop F. Houlston and Son Published between 1828 and 1840 746053694

div.p: Published between 1828 and 1840, A Short History of Birds and Beasts is a small catalog of birds, insects, and mammals, with images and brief descriptions of each animal underneath—intended for a child audience. The descriptions are presented in a nursery rhyme-like form rather than as a scientific report in order to further audience engagement with the text. Additionally, the pocket-sized nature of the text’s physical form lends itself to portability. With its compact size, variety of fonts, and detailed imagery, A Short History of Birds and Beasts combines rhyming verse with visual imagery to ultimately create a text that is both entertaining and educational in its message. This edition seeks to draw attention to how the combination of visual and textual elements within children’s literature can play a role in audience engagement and understanding of a text. In doing so, a unique perspective on the historical evolution of children’s literature becomes more distinctly illuminated. To do this, we chose to utilize a diplomatic transcription of the text to highlight this evolution as distinctly as possible. In order to maintain the combination of the textual and visual, the images and fonts used in the original edition were transcribed within our digital edition. Furthermore, by digitizing text previously attainable only through the UW Special Collections, we hope to increase the accessibility of our text in a wider, not purely archival, context.

docTitle.titlePart:
A
SHORT HISTORY
OF
BIRDS AND BEASTS,
FOR THE
Amusement and Instruction
OF
CHILDREN.
ADORNED WITH CUTS.

div.head: THE COW.

lg.l: Early the milkmaid to the meadow hies,
And the red Cow her empty pail supplies.

div.p:
This is the good-natured Cow to which we are all so much obliged. She comes, poor thing! in the morning, and brings her udder full of milk for
our breakfast, and the same at night for our supper. To her we are indebted for our custards, cheesecakes, curds, and cream, as well as for our milk, butter, and cheese.

div.head: THE NIGHTINGALE.

lg.l: The Nightingale doth sweetly sing,
To welcome in the cheerful spring.

div.p: What a pretty bird the Nightingale is! How sweetly she sings! I could wish 'twas summer all the year for the sake of her good company.

div.head: THE LAMB.

lg.l: The little Lamb doth skip and play,
Always merry, always gay.

div.p: See the little Lamb! how innocent he looks! he never did any harm, and therefore is beloved by every body: but the fox and the wolf, who are always in mischief, are hated and despised.

div.head: THE LION.

lg.l: The Lion ranges round the wood,
And makes the lesser beasts his food:
Thus tyrants on their subject prey,
And rule with arbitrary sway.

div.p:
Though the Lion is such a strong devouring creature, yet Daniel was thrown into a den among several of
them, and received no harm. For he was punished on account of his religion and virtue, he prayed unto God, and the Lord delivered him.

div.head: THE WHALE.

lg.l: The Whale's the monarch of the main,
(As is the Lion of the plain:)
He keeps the lesser fish in awe,
And, tyrant-like, his will's his law.

div.p:
When the prophet Jonah attempted to fly over sea from the presence of the Lord, there arose a great storm, and
he being cast into the deep, was swallowed by this great fish, in whose belly he repented sincerely, and prayed unto God; wherefore the Lord commanded the fish, and he swam to shore, and cast him upon dry land.

div.head: THE BUTTERFLY.

lg.l: The Butterfly in gaudy dress,
The worthless coxcomb doth express,
Who not regarding whence he rose,
Is proud of what?-- of his fine clothes

div.p:
This gaudy Butterfly owes its being to a poor worm, and has nothing to boast of but his fine wings, which perhaps will
be lost the first frosty day: and then his case will be much like the cox-comb's, who having lost his fine hat and bag wig, has nothing to support him but a head full of emptiness.

div.head: THE CROCODILE.

lg.l: The Crocodile, with watery eyes,
O'er man and every creature cries,
Then feeds with pleasure on his prey;
So hypocrites their friends betray

div.p:
This terrible creature is said to weep over his prey before he devours it, as if he was unwilling to destroy any thing; but in truth, that whining is only to
bring other creatures to see what's the matter, that Mr. Crocodile may get another snap for his belly.

div.head: THE ASS.

lg.l: The Ass, tho' mean, will by his bray
Oblige your horse to run away.

div.p: Though this animal makes such a mean figure, yes, Samson, with the jawbone of an Ass, slew a thousand men. But then the Lord was with him, and God Almighty can do any thing.

div.head: THE ANT.

lg.l: The little Ant no labour spares,
Wisely preventing future cares;
For ere the hoary frost comes on,
Her stock's laid up, and business done.

div.p:
This little creature was a great favourite with the wise king Solomon, who much admired her industry and care-
fulness, and recommends her to the consideration of every idle person. "Arise, though sluggard, go to the Ant, consider her ways, and be wise."

div.note: We edited the line groups of verse into quatrains separate from the following prose See source 4.
Section 13: The Lion references the biblical story of Daniel in the lions’ den.
Section 15: The Whale references the biblical story of Jonah, who was swallowed by a whale.
Section 21: The Ass references the biblical story of Samson.
Section 22: The Ant references and quotes the biblical king Solomon.
